hints: Look closely at how flat or how tightly rolled each leaf is, and notice that layer Y is always on the inside of the curve.
Remember what makes a xerophytic leaf roll up: loss of water from the upper hinge cells makes them flaccid, so link turgidity to higher (less negative) water potential.
walkthrough:
**Observe the rolling**

Look at P, R and S side by side. P is completely flat and open. S is partly curled. R is very tightly rolled into almost a tube.

Layer Y is the inner layer in R and S, so it is the layer controlling the rolling.

**Link rolling to turgor in layer Y**

This is the classic xerophyte response, for example in marram grass. When water is plentiful, the cells in the upper layer take up water by osmosis, become turgid and hold the leaf flat.

When water is scarce, those cells lose water, become flaccid and shrink, pulling the leaf into a roll to hide stomata.

**Rank the water potentials**

More water in the cell means higher, less negative, water potential. Less water means lower, more negative, water potential.

So P (flat, fully turgid) has the highest water potential. R (tightly rolled, most flaccid) has the lowest water potential. S is in between: lower than P but higher than R.

options.A: Correct. P is highest, R is lowest, and S is intermediate (lower than P but higher than R). This matches flat to tightly rolled.
options.B: False. S cannot be higher than P because S is already partly rolled, showing some water loss from layer Y.
options.C: False. It reverses the pattern. P cannot be lower than R, as the flat leaf must have the most turgid cells with highest water potential.
options.D: False. It gives P the lowest water potential, but a flat open leaf needs high turgor and high water potential in layer Y.
